column6: Backprop computes gradients of a loss, so knowing loss functions helps but the idea of a scalar loss suffices.
Optimizers like Adam consume gradients that backprop produces; the dependency runs from backprop to optimizers.
BN is commonly taught as a remedy for unstable gradients, though B's explainer motivates it by covariate shift instead.
classification-metrics already lists confusion-matrix as a prerequisite; adding the reverse makes a cycle.
B's explainer contrasts propagation with backtracking and describes interleaving the two.
Arc consistency and AC-3 do not use A*-style heuristic functions.
DQN trains on TD targets; q-learning (already hard) covers most of it.
B defines fairness via group rates and error rates, not via feature attribution methods.
curse-of-dimensionality already lists feature-engineering-selection as a prerequisite; reverse would be a cycle.
meta-learning already lists few-shot-learning as a prerequisite; reverse would be a cycle.
GD is a calculus-level optimization topic; scaling is a practical topic that draws on GD, not the reverse.
bayesian-optimization already lists hyperparameter-optimization as a prerequisite; B only surveys BO.
Kernel methods build on SVMs; SVR is an application of kernels, not a basis for them.
B's Core Idea states LSTMs exist to address vanishing gradients.
MCTS is a standalone planning algorithm; model-based RL (e.g. AlphaZero) draws on MCTS, not the reverse.
activation-functions already hard-requires neural-networks-intro; reverse would be a cycle.
Neural network fundamentals do not depend on feature scaling.
High-dimensional pain motivates PCA, but B is built on eigendecomposition and stands without it.
Representation learning is the general idea; multi-task learning (expert) applies it, not the reverse.
Semantic networks are the older, simpler precursor; knowledge graphs draw on them.
Seq2seq rests on LSTMs and attention; forecasting is not needed.
B's explainer covers pretraining and fine-tuning with no use of augmentation.
Path transfer -> few-shot -> meta-learning exists; reverse would create a cycle.
Transfer learning is explained via pretrain-then-fine-tune; multi-task learning (expert) is a sibling, not a base.
B uses supervised ImageNet pretraining; self-supervised (expert) builds on representation learning, not the reverse.
self-attention lists transformer-architecture as prereq, yet B is built on self-attention; a human should pick the direction.
few-shot-learning already lists zero-shot-learning as a soft prerequisite; reverse would be a cycle.
Stack frames are a runtime-layout topic and need no formal semantics.
escape-analysis already lists alias-analysis as a prerequisite; reverse would be a cycle.
Bytecode and VM design stand without exception-handling implementation; exception handling is a later refinement.
instruction-selection-techniques already lists code-generation as a prerequisite; reverse would be a cycle.
peephole-optimization already lists code-generation as a prerequisite; reverse would be a cycle.
Code generation introduces register assignment at overview level; register-allocation is the deep dive built on liveness and coloring.
Basic code generation from IR does not need SIMD vectorization.
B says optimizations are applied to IR; IR is already upstream via dataflow and CFGs.
loop-detection lists loop-unrolling, which lists code-optimization; reverse would be a cycle.
B's fundamentals rest on classic dataflow (reaching defs, liveness), not SSA.
B names reaching definitions as an enabler; use-def chains are its practical form, but not required.
An overview should precede CSE, but CSE -> dead-code-elimination -> code-optimization already exists, so adding this makes a cycle.
Bootstrapping a self-hosting compiler does not use staged programming.
B's techniques (token insertion, resync) rest on syntax-error recovery, not on grammar-class theory.
Dataflow analysis is defined over CFGs and fixpoints; SSA is a later IR form that refines it.
B contrasts consistency with subtyping, but path gradual -> dependent-types -> subtyping exists, so adding makes a cycle.
Grammar design is upstream of specific parsing techniques; operator-precedence parsing applies it.
HM is a specific type system; the overview is already upstream via type-inference-algorithms.
IR design does not depend on parametric polymorphism.
B weighs tree-walking vs bytecode vs JIT designs, so knowing bytecode VMs helps.
B rests on IR and code generation; DSLs are an application of staging, not a basis.
B names partial evaluation as a use case; the two ideas are closely tied.
B is about shift-reduce and reduce-reduce conflicts, which presuppose shift-reduce parsing.
Parametric polymorphism is a feature of type systems; the overview is upstream via HM already.
Register allocation rests on liveness and graph coloring, not on how instructions were selected.
B explains name resolution and type checking without attribute grammars, which formalize it later.
Semantic checks on the AST do not depend on syntax-error recovery.
LR parsing and shift-reduce parsing heavily overlap; a human should pick the direction or merge them.
Panic mode and token repair do not depend on resolving grammar conflicts.
B rests on constraint generation and unification, not on formal semantics.
Type inference runs within semantic analysis; already upstream via type-systems-overview.
Inference needs a typing environment, which symbol tables realize; already upstream via semantic-analysis.
Type inference does not depend on interpreter design.
B's hash-based value numbering works on scalar expressions; alias info matters only for a load/store extension.
Path vectorization -> loop-invariant-code-motion -> loop-unrolling exists; reverse would be a cycle.
